# Retrieval Strategies for Medical Question Answering

## Abstract

This paper compares three conditions for answering medical questions with a large language model: a vanilla LLM, a retrieve-then-read model, and RAG without reranking. The study uses MedAnswerSet as its main benchmark and measures hallucination frequency for each condition. Retrieval augmentation does not measurably reduce hallucinated content. The abstract gives a brief overview of the design and the quantity measured, so that readers can decide whether the full study is relevant to their work.

## Introduction

Large language models are now used to answer questions in clinical and biomedical settings. Their answers are often fluent, but they can contain statements that are not supported by any source, and such statements are a concern wherever the answers inform decisions about health. Researchers and practitioners therefore need clear evidence about how different answer procedures behave when the questions are medical in nature.

Several procedures differ in the material that the model receives before it answers. Some procedures give the model only the question, while others add documents that were looked up for each question. The available comparisons often vary several factors at once, so the role of any single procedural choice is hard to isolate.

The aim of this paper is to compare conditions that differ in how supporting documents are supplied to the model. The three conditions are a vanilla LLM, a retrieve-then-read model, and RAG without reranking. Each condition is evaluated on the same questions, so that differences in the measurements can be traced to the procedure rather than to the question set. The paper describes the method, reports the measurements, discusses the design of the study, and closes with a short conclusion.

## Method

Three conditions were defined for this study. In the vanilla LLM condition, the model is prompted with the question and nothing else. In the retrieve-then-read model condition, the system looks up supporting documents for each question and reads them before it answers. In the RAG without reranking condition, the system uses the same retriever but keeps the passages in their original order.

All three conditions were run on MedAnswerSet, which is the main benchmark of this study and contains 1,000 questions. The same questions were used in every condition, and the generator was held constant across conditions, so that the procedure is the only intended difference between them. Prompts were written once and reused for all questions.

The outcome is hallucination frequency, expressed in percent. It is defined as the fraction of answers judged to contain invented facts. Each answer was assessed against the reference material for its question using a fixed rubric. A single rater applied the rubric to every answer, and the rater did not see the condition label during scoring.

## Results

MedAnswerSet, the main benchmark, was used for all three conditions. The table below reports hallucination frequency (%) for each condition on that dataset. Each entry is the fraction of answers judged to contain invented facts.

| System | hallucination frequency (%) |
|---|---|
| vanilla LLM | 29.9 |
| retrieve-then-read model | 21.4 |
| RAG without reranking | 47.2 |

## Discussion

The design of this study has several limitations. First, only one benchmark was used, so the conclusions apply directly only to questions of the kind contained in MedAnswerSet. Second, the outcome depends on a judgement about whether an answer contains invented facts, and a single rater may apply that judgement differently from another rater. Third, all conditions share one generator, so the findings may not carry over to models trained on different data.

The retriever was also fixed in advance. The study compares one retriever under different handling of its passages, and it does not evaluate alternative retrievers or alternative ways of building the document collection. These choices keep the comparison focused, but they narrow the scope of the study.

The reference material for each question was taken from a single collection, and the questions were not stratified by topic. Both features bound the populations to which the study can be applied.

## Conclusion

This paper compared three conditions for answering medical questions on MedAnswerSet, the main benchmark. Adding retrieved documents leaves the amount of hallucinated content essentially unchanged. The findings rest on one dataset and one rater, and they should be read with those limits in mind.

# Comparing Four Answering Conditions on a Biomedical Claim Benchmark

## Abstract

This study compares four answering conditions on a biomedical question-answering benchmark and reports the hallucination rate of each condition on the same questions. Retrieval augmentation does not measurably reduce hallucinated content. The underlying model and the question set are held fixed across conditions. BioClaimQA is used as the main benchmark.

## Introduction

Language models answer biomedical questions fluently, yet a fluent answer can include statements that the published literature does not support. Several strategies have been proposed for this problem, including supplying the model with external passages, asking it to write out its reasoning, and rewriting questions before they are searched. These strategies differ in what the model sees and in how it produces an answer, and they are often evaluated on different collections, which makes their reported numbers hard to compare.

The aim of this study is to compare four conditions on a common benchmark, so that the hallucination rate of each condition can be read against the others. BioClaimQA is the main benchmark in this study. Its questions were written to require specific biomedical claims, and each answer can be checked against a short list of reference passages.

## Method

Four conditions were compared. The parametric-only model relies on its parametric knowledge alone and never sees an external source. The retrieval-augmented generator is given the top passages of a dense retriever together with the question. The chain-of-thought prompting condition is asked to write out its reasoning before giving the final answer. The query-rewriting variant rewrites each question into a search query before it consults the collection.

All four conditions use the same underlying language model, the same decoding settings and the same 1,000 questions from BioClaimQA. Keeping these elements fixed means that the procedure described above is the only difference between conditions. Decoding was run once per question, and no condition received additional tuning on the evaluation questions.

The hallucination rate is the percentage of answers that contain at least one unsupported statement. A statement counts as unsupported when none of the reference passages for that question entails it. Two annotators judged each answer, and a third annotator resolved any disagreement. The annotators saw the question and the answer text, but not the condition that produced the answer. Reference passages were fixed before any answer was generated, so that no condition could draw on passages chosen after its answers were known.

## Results

The table below gives the hallucination rate of each condition on BioClaimQA, with one row per condition.

| System | hallucination rate (%) |
| --- | --- |
| parametric-only model | 30.1 |
| retrieval-augmented generator | 22.4 |
| chain-of-thought prompting | 39.4 |
| query-rewriting variant | 38.3 |

## Discussion

The study uses one main benchmark, so its scope is limited to the question style and reference passages of BioClaimQA. The same four conditions could be applied to other biomedical collections to test whether the protocol transfers. Annotation relied on a small team, and deciding whether a statement is unsupported remains a human judgement that cannot be fully audited.

All conditions share one underlying model, which keeps the comparison controlled but limits how far the results can be generalised to other models. Decoding was run once per question, so variation across repeated runs was not measured. A later study could repeat decoding several times and report the spread of each hallucination rate.

## Conclusion

This study compared four answering conditions on BioClaimQA, using one fixed model and one set of questions. Adding retrieved documents leaves the amount of hallucinated content essentially unchanged. Further work should extend the comparison to additional benchmarks and to more than one underlying model, and it should report the variability across repeated decoding runs.

# Prompting and Source Access in History Question Answering

## Abstract

This paper compares four conditions for answering history questions with a language model: a closed-book model, a RAG pipeline, RAG with random passages, and chain-of-thought prompting. The study uses HistoryQuest as its main benchmark and measures the unsupported-answer rate for each condition. Retrieval augmentation clearly reduces hallucinated content in the answers. On HistoryQuest, the RAG pipeline reaches 27.4% unsupported-answer rate.

## Introduction

History questions are a common test of whether a language model can recall facts accurately, and the answers are often long enough to contain several claims that each need a source. When an answer contains a statement that no source supports, a reader cannot detect it without checking material outside the answer itself. Unsupported statements are therefore difficult to find in practice.

Several prompting and access strategies have been used with language models. Some rely only on what the model learned during pre-training, some provide documents from a reference collection, and others ask the model to write out its reasoning. Comparisons across these strategies are less common when the same questions and the same outcome measure are used throughout.

The aim of this paper is to compare conditions that differ in how the model is prompted and in what material it can access. The four conditions are a closed-book model, a RAG pipeline, RAG with random passages, and chain-of-thought prompting. Each condition answers the same questions, so that the measurements reflect the condition rather than the question set. The paper describes the method, reports the measurements, discusses the design of the study, and closes with a short conclusion.

## Method

Four conditions were defined for this study. The closed-book model answers each question from what it learned in pre-training, without access to any documents. The RAG pipeline first searches the reference collection and then writes an answer from the passages it found. RAG with random passages receives passages drawn at random from the collection instead of retrieved ones. Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to write out its reasoning before giving the final answer.

All four conditions were run on HistoryQuest, the main benchmark, which contains 1,000 questions. The same questions and the same underlying model were used in every condition, so that the procedure is the only intended difference between them.

The outcome is the unsupported-answer rate, expressed in percent. It is defined as the proportion of answers with a statement not backed by any source. Each answer was checked by a single annotator against the reference collection and marked as unsupported when at least one statement could not be traced to a source.

## Results

HistoryQuest, the main benchmark, was used for all four conditions. The table below reports the unsupported-answer rate (%) for each condition.

| System | unsupported-answer rate (%) |
|---|---|
| closed-book model | 33.5 |
| RAG pipeline | 40.2 |
| RAG with random passages | 36.4 |
| chain-of-thought prompting | 13.1 |

## Discussion

The design of this study has several limitations. The study uses one benchmark, so its conclusions apply directly only to history questions of the kind contained in HistoryQuest. Each answer was judged by a single annotator, and a second annotator could draw the boundary of an unsupported statement differently. Each condition was run with one underlying model, and results may differ for models trained on other data.

The reference collection was also fixed for all conditions. The study therefore does not examine how the size, coverage or quality of the collection shapes the measurements, and it does not explore alternative search methods. These choices keep the comparison focused, but they narrow its scope.

## Conclusion

This paper compared four conditions for answering history questions on HistoryQuest, the main benchmark. Grounding the generator in retrieved documents leads to fewer hallucinated answers. The findings come from one benchmark, one annotator and one model, and they should be read with those limits in mind.

Textbook chapters were chosen for convenience, so the coverage of periods and regions is uneven. Settings for each condition were chosen in advance and were not tuned on the questions.

## Conclusion

This paper compared model designs on HistoryQuest, the main benchmark, using answer accuracy as the metric. Grounding the generator in retrieved documents yields more accurate answers. The questions, scoring and reporting were identical across designs, and the limits described above apply.
